$comment: The shared conformance corpus for the agent inbox protocol.
This file is DATA, not code, and that is the whole point. The two
implementations of docs/protocol.md in this repository are a Python CLI
(packages/base/bin/inbox) and a TypeScript application (packages/deck).
There is no code they can share, so the only thing that can hold them
together is a body of inputs and expected outputs that both must satisfy,
each through a thin adapter in its own language.
Read docs/conformance.md before adding a case. The short version:
expect      what docs/protocol.md REQUIRES. Normative. Never edit it to
match an implementation; that is the failure this file
exists to prevent.
deviations  a per-implementation record of a KNOWN, REVIEWED departure
from `expect`. A deviation is a defect with a name, not a
permission slip. The runner asserts the implementation still
produces exactly the recorded wrong answer, so a deviation
that changes shape fails, AND it asserts the implementation
does NOT produce the right answer, so a deviation that gets
FIXED also fails, forcing its own record to be deleted.
A waiver cannot outlive the thing it documents.
Canonical block shape, which both adapters project onto:
ts, sender, status, subject   the four header fields
bodyRaw                       everything after the header line, up to the
start of the next block, trimmed
bodyRaw rather than each implementation's presentation body, deliberately.
The two clean bodies for display in legitimately different ways (the CLI
strips every standalone '---' line; the application preserves body-internal
ones and lifts a YAML metadata region out of the body). Comparing display
bodies would bury real boundary drift under differences that are intended.
bodyRaw is derivable from both without touching either's cleaning, and it is
exactly the value that moves when block boundaries drift.
A block whose header line does not parse is not a block: both adapters drop
it, matching protocol section 4.

cases.why: The plain 'space hyphen space' separator form.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: hello there

first body

cases.why: The em-dash separator form, U+2014. Written as a JSON \u escape so this file holds no literal em-dash; the parsed value is the real character.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z — from: bob — status: sent — subject: hello

body

cases.why: The en-dash separator form, U+2013.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z – from: bob – status: sent – subject: hello

body

cases.why: Section 5 says matching MUST be case insensitive, and 5.2 says a reader SHOULD lower case the status for comparison. An all-caps header is written by other tools and must still parse.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - FROM: bob - STATUS: SENT - SUBJECT: shouty

body

deck.reason: The application's HEADER_RE carries no `i` flag, so an all-caps header does not parse at all and the block is dropped. Protocol section 5 says matching MUST be case insensitive. A header written in another case by any other tool is invisible to the application: the message is on disk and never renders.

cases.why: Conformance point 2. The sender is a run of non-whitespace, so a dash inside the NAME is in the same character class as the separator after it. The field labels are what disambiguate on backtracking. Section 5.1 claims this was verified empirically rather than assumed; this case is that verification.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: al–ice - status: sent - subject: hi

body

cases.why: The subject is the remainder of the line, so any dash in it must never be re-read as a separator and truncate the value.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: a – b - c

body

cases.why: The subject MAY be empty, and section 5 makes whitespace after the label optional.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject:

body

deck.reason: The application's HEADER_RE requires at least one space after `subject:` (`subject:\s+`). Protocol section 5 makes the whitespace after a field label OPTIONAL and the subject MAY be empty, so a header ending in a bare `subject:` is valid and the application drops it. The CLI writes a trailing space for an empty subject, which is why this has not bitten in practice; any other writer that does not is invisible.

cases.why: The spelling both writers actually emit for an empty subject: the label, one space, end of line. Its sibling above covers the bare-label spelling, and the application's deviation there is exactly why this one needs a case of its own - the answer recorded for the application on that case is already 'no blocks', so a reader that stopped recognising THIS line too would leave the sibling passing and say nothing. The application did precisely that for a day: its block-boundary test trimmed the line before matching, which took off the one space its own grammar requires, and a message with no subject was absorbed into the block above it.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: 

body

cases.why: Both delivery states parse. Section 6: status has exactly two values.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: bob - status: read - subject: seen

body

cases.why: Ordering is by position in the file, never by timestamp (section 9.2). The second block here is deliberately older than the first.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:05:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: two

second body

## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: alice - status: read - subject: one

first body

cases.why: THE ONE THAT LOSES MESSAGES. A column-0 '## ' line that fails the header grammar does NOT begin a block: it is body content of the preceding block. An implementation that treats every '## ' line as a boundary silently truncates any message whose author typed a markdown heading. The bytes on disk are intact; the loss happens on every read.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: plan

intro line
## Options
the part that must not vanish

expect.subject: plan
expect.bodyRaw:
intro line
## Options
the part that must not vanish

cases.why: A pseudo header absorbed into one body must not shift or split the block that follows it.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: alice - status: sent - subject: mine

my own note
## Interlude heading, not a header

## 2026-08-13T10:05:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: theirs

bob's note

expect.subject: mine
expect.bodyRaw:

## Interlude heading, not a header

cases.why: A pseudo header before any real block is leading content, not a block.
cases.input:
## leading pseudo header

## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: hi

real body

cases.why: Conformance point 10. A reader MUST tolerate malformed content and MUST NOT repair it. The status-less header here is header-shaped but ungrammatical, so it is body content, and the surrounding prose survives.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: real

real body line
## 2026-08-13T10:01:00Z - from: bob - subject: no status field
prose sitting after the pseudo header

expect.subject: real
expect.bodyRaw:
real body line
## 2026-08-13T10:01:00Z - from: bob - subject: no status field
prose sitting after the pseudo header

deck.reason: A DIFFERENT CAUSE from the one this record used to carry. Both readers took block boundaries off every '## ' line until 2026-08-14 and this case failed on both for that reason; the boundary rule is now correct in both, and what is left here is the application's HEADER_RE alone. It makes the whole `status: <value> -` segment OPTIONAL, tolerated on READ because a header that dropped it used to blank the timestamp in the UI (the 2026-06-11 queue incident), so the status-less line in this input PARSES for the application and legitimately opens a block. The CLI requires status and treats the same line as body. The two now disagree with each other about what is a header, which is a grammar-tolerance question for section 5, not a boundary one: fixing it means deciding whether the protocol admits a status-less header at all, and then changing the reader that is wrong. Nothing is lost here in either implementation, the prose is attributed differently.

expect.subject: no status field
expect.bodyRaw: prose sitting after the pseudo header

cases.why: Section 5 defines the timestamp as a run of non-whitespace characters and only SHOULD it be ISO 8601. Section 9.1 states plainly that a block with an unparseable timestamp is still a block. An implementation that validates the timestamp and rejects the block loses the message.
cases.input:
## not-a-timestamp - from: bob - status: sent - subject: odd clock

body

deck.reason: The application validates the timestamp with Date.parse and returns ok:false when it fails. Protocol section 5 defines the timestamp as a run of non-whitespace characters and only SHOULD it be ISO 8601, and section 9.1 states plainly that a block with an unparseable timestamp is still a block. The application loses the message rather than rendering it with an odd timestamp.

cases.why: The header the whole of section 8.3 is about. It must PARSE correctly here (the write-side hazard is tested separately, in each implementation's own suite, because it is a mutation rather than a projection).
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: status:sentinel - status: sent - subject: hi

body

cases.why: Section 4 says a block begins at a line that starts with '## ' AT COLUMN 0. An indented one is body content.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: hi

body line
  ## 2026-08-13T10:05:00Z - from: alice - status: sent - subject: indented
more body

expect.subject: hi
expect.bodyRaw:
body line
  ## 2026-08-13T10:05:00Z - from: alice - status: sent - subject: indented
more body

deck.reason: The application strips LEADING whitespace off a line before matching the header grammar against it, so an INDENTED header-shaped line that is otherwise well formed begins a block. Protocol section 4 anchors a block at column 0. This is the opposite direction from the CLI, whose scan is anchored there and correctly reads the indented line as body, so the two implementations disagree with each other here as well as with the specification. (This text described the boundary test as `line.trim().startsWith('## ')` until 2026-08-17, two fixes after that stopped being what it did; the behaviour recorded below never moved.)

cases.why: An earlier block carrying multi-byte UTF-8 must not disturb the parse of a later one. Accented characters (two UTF-8 bytes, one UTF-16 unit) and an emoji (four UTF-8 bytes, two UTF-16 units) drift by different amounts, so both are present.
cases.input:
## 2026-08-13T10:00:00Z - from: alice - status: sent - subject: café naïve 🚀

résumé 🎯 first body

## 2026-08-13T10:05:00Z - from: bob - status: sent - subject: second

plain body

cases.why: A thread file with no blocks parses to no blocks, rather than erroring.
Leading content with no block header at all is not a block.

just some prose
with no header line
